content.text: Rates of reaction
Recall: which units measure gas volume and time?

content.text: Today we are learning to
Calculate the mean rate of reaction from the volume of gas produced over a measured time, using cm³/s.
Describe how to investigate the effect of hydrochloric acid concentration on its reaction with magnesium, measuring gas volume over time and controlling the mass of magnesium and temperature.
Explain why increasing hydrochloric acid concentration increases the rate of reaction with magnesium, using collision theory and the frequency of successful collisions.
Measure gas as the reaction happens
Magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
Collect hydrogen in a gas syringe.
Start the timer when acid meets magnesium.
Record gas volume every 10 seconds.

elements.name: Photo
elements.alt: A conical flask containing acid and magnesium is connected to a gas syringe, with bubbles visible in the liquid.
elements.request: An airtight conical flask containing hydrochloric acid and magnesium ribbon, connected through a bung and delivery tube to a horizontally clamped gas syringe. Hydrogen moves the plunger outwards; the syringe plunger is free to move.. Gas syringe. Delivery tube. Bung. Hydrochloric acid

content.text: Worked example: mean rate
Gas volume rises from 0 to 48 cm³ in 20 s.
Mean rate = gas volume ÷ time
Mean rate = 48 ÷ 20
Mean rate = 2.4 cm³/s
This is the average over the measured interval.
Calculate the mean rate
Gas volume rises from 0 to 54 cm³ in 20 s. Calculate the mean rate.
Write the unit of your answer.
Explain what your answer tells you about gas produced per second.
Write the formula, substitution and answer.
Change concentration fairly
Use 25 cm³ acid; vary only its concentration.
Keep magnesium mass and temperature the same.
Record gas volume every 10 s for 60 s.
Repeat each concentration three times; calculate means.

elements.alt: Acid concentration varies between three trials; magnesium mass is 0.04 g and temperature is 20 degrees Celsius in each.

content.text: Plan the investigation
Compare 0.5 and 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. What will you change and measure?
How will you control magnesium mass and temperature?
How will you collect gas, time readings and make results more reliable?
Write a short method using a gas syringe.
Why does concentration matter?
Higher concentration means more acid particles in each cm³.
Acid particles hit the magnesium more often.
A successful collision has enough energy to react.
More successful collisions per second increase the rate.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Two equal-volume panels compare acid concentration around identical magnesium surfaces at 20 °C. The higher-concentration panel has twice as many acid particles and more contacts.

content.text: More concentrated does not mean faster particles
Both acids are at 20 °C. Their particles have the same average kinetic energy.
What changes
Compare equal volumes of 0.5 mol/dm³ and 1.0 mol/dm³ acid beside identical magnesium surfaces. The more concentrated acid has more particles; representative motion arrows are the same length.
Why rate rises
More successful collisions occur each second.
Choose the best explanation
At the same temperature, why does more concentrated acid react faster with magnesium?
A
Each acid particle has more energy.
B
Every collision now causes a reaction.
C
Acid particles move faster.
D
More successful collisions occur each second.
Use the evidence
In 20 s, acid A produces 24 cm³ gas and acid B produces 40 cm³. Both start at 0 cm³. Calculate both mean rates.
Both use 0.04 g magnesium, 25 cm³ acid and 20 °C. B is more concentrated. Explain its higher rate.
Stretch: both acids are in excess. Predict whether the final gas volumes differ. Explain using the magnesium mass.
Calculate, then explain using successful collisions.
Can this comparison be trusted?
Trial A uses 0.5 mol/dm³ acid at 20 °C; B uses 1.0 mol/dm³ at 30 °C. B is faster. Can concentration alone explain this?
Both use 25 cm³ acid and 0.04 g magnesium. Describe a fair repeat using gas-volume readings.
Predict the result of your fair repeat. Explain using successful collisions per second.
Evaluate the claim and improve the investigation.
